questions.question: What happens when you access a property that doesn't exist directly on an object?
options: JavaScript immediately returns undefined with no further lookup
The engine walks up the object's prototype chain looking for the property before giving up and returning undefined
It checks global variables with the same name
questions.explanation: Property lookup checks the object itself first, then follows the chain of prototypes until the property is found or the chain ends.

questions.question: What is the difference between an object's "prototype" and a function's `.prototype` property?
options: They are exactly the same thing with two names
An object's prototype is the object it delegates to for lookups; a function's `.prototype` property is the template object used to set up instances created with `new` from that function
Only arrow functions have a .prototype property
Prototypes were removed in modern JavaScript
questions.explanation: These are related but distinct: `.prototype` on a constructor function becomes the prototype of objects it constructs via `new`.

questions.question: What three things does `new Animal("Rex")` do?
options: It only calls the Animal function with no side effects
Creates a new empty object, links that object's prototype to Animal.prototype, and runs Animal with `this` bound to the new object
It copies all of Animal's methods directly onto the new object
It creates a completely independent copy of the Animal function
questions.explanation: The `new` operator creates an object, wires up the prototype link, then invokes the constructor function with that object as `this`.

questions.question: What does `class ... extends ...` fundamentally compile down to?
options: A brand-new inheritance model unrelated to prototypes
The same constructor-function-and-prototype-chain mechanism, just with cleaner, stricter syntax
Multiple independent copies of the parent class's methods
A runtime-only feature with no connection to how `new` and prototypes work
questions.explanation: class/extends links prototype objects together exactly as manually chaining constructor functions via Object.create would — it's syntactic sugar, not a separate object model.
